candidates.rationale: Top performer in the batch (fitness 10.34, stability 1.00, turnover charge only 0.004), so none of the three named failure modes (regime, turnover, half-life) apply. Its real weakness is structural: this is the close/low/high range-position family the working memory flags as over-mined this round, and it sits closest of any parent to an archive neighbor (rho 0.596) that also uses a high/low range. Per the memory's own remedy (normalize by dispersion, not range, rather than tweaking a parameter), replaced only the max-min range denominator with TS_STD($low, 21). Dropped $high entirely, decorrelating from the range-based archive neighbor while leaving the numerator's close-vs-recent-low logic untouched.

Textbook regime problem: positive in 12 of 14 years, negative in exactly two (2003, 2006). The raw ROA level is a static profitability snapshot whose cross-sectional efficacy plausibly flips with valuation regime. Swapped the level for its own one-quarter change (63 trading days), a profitability-trend measure that is typically more regime-robust than the level, keeping the single field and the RANK wrapper untouched.

Shortest IC half-life in the batch (3.0 days): this oscillator is being asked to predict further out than its 15-day construction can sustain. Lengthened both the min-window and the std-window together, 15 to 63 days (kept matched, not mismatched, per this island's ratio rule), safely under the 126-day coverage ceiling. Same field, same shape, just slower, which should extend persistence and cut the day-to-day churn behind the 0.273 turnover.

Regime problem (negative IC in 3 of 14 years: 2003, 2005, 2007) plus the tightest archive proximity in the batch, rho 0.779 against a dollar-volume-based neighbor, close to the 0.80 cutoff. The absolute liquidity level is the common cause. Relabeled the one operator, TS_MEAN to TS_DELTA, same field, same 21-day window, turning an absolute level into a liquidity trend that should be less regime-dependent and less correlated with the archive's level-based neighbor.

Clear regime break: positive IC every year 2000-2009, then negative in all four of 2010-2013, consistent with the well-documented post-2009 decay of ultra-short reversal signals. The same 2-day reversal term is also the likely driver of this batch's second-highest turnover (0.516) and a short 4.1-day half-life. Widened only that window, 2 to 10 days, to slow the reversal term down. Left the volume-ratio co-factor and the multiplicative structure untouched, since this island's memory already warns that restructuring that combination pattern tends to cancel signal.

Highest turnover charge in the batch (0.021) against one of the weakest raw ICs (t=2.08): paying costs it doesn't earn back. Half-life is actually long (>63d), so the persistent part of the signal is fine; the problem is a noisy single-day numerator judged against a smooth 21-day baseline. Smoothed only the numerator over 5 days, kept the 21-day baseline and field set unchanged, to cut day-to-day churn while preserving the current-vs-baseline contrast.

Worst regime stability in the batch (0.57, negative in 6 of 14 years, including 2001 and 2009, textbook momentum-crash years). This is 126-day risk-adjusted momentum with no gap between the return-measurement window and today, so the freshest month is exactly the part most exposed to crash-driven reversal. Applied the standard skip-the-most-recent-month fix by lagging only the return-sum numerator 21 days, leaving the contemporaneous volatility scaling in the denominator untouched.

Weakest factor in the batch: t=1.18, the only parent below conventional significance, plus mediocre stability (0.71) with both of the most recent years, 2012 and 2013, negative. The working memory flags this exact piecewise return-count shape at a 21-day window and recommends a different window before resubmitting. Changed only the window, 21 to 63, to reduce the noise in the up-day count so the cross-sectional ranking is less driven by single-day flips.

prompt:
You are proposing quantitative factor expressions for US large-cap equities.

Universe and data
- S&P 500 point-in-time constituents, roughly 500 names per day.
- Daily bars only, plus point-in-time quarterly fundamentals stamped from the
  report date. Every field is referenced with a leading `$`:
    $open $high $low $close $adj_close $volume $dollar_volume $return
    $roa $roe $operating_margin $leverage $asset_turnover
    $book_per_share $earnings_per_share $accrual_gap
  A bare name such as `close` is not a field and will be rejected.
- Execution convention: the signal is computed after the close of day T and the
  position is entered at the open of T+1.
- The window these factors are fitted and judged on runs from 2000 to 2013.
  Do not reason about anything later; you will never be shown a number from
  outside that window.

Syntax
- Operators are function calls: TS_MEAN, TS_STD, TS_MAX, TS_MIN, TS_RANK,
  TS_DELTA, TS_CORR, TS_COV, TS_SUM, TS_PRODUCT, TS_ARGMAX, TS_ARGMIN,
  TS_DECAY_LINEAR, EMA, DELAY, DELTA, RANK, ZSCORE, CS_RANK, CS_ZSCORE,
  CS_DEMEAN, IF, IF_ELSE, MIN, MAX, ABS, SIGN, LOG, LN, SQRT, POWER, BOUND,
  COUNT.
- Lookback windows must be positive integer literals, e.g. TS_MEAN($close, 21).
- Guard every division with a small epsilon: `/ (TS_STD($close, 21) + 1e-8)`.
- Well-formed example: -RANK(TS_CORR(RANK($close), RANK($volume), 5))

Hard limits every proposal must satisfy, or it is rejected before it is scored
- at most 200 characters
- at most 5 distinct `$fields`
- at most 4 free numeric constants (lookback windows and
  the 1e-8 epsilon guard do not count)
- expression tree depth at most 6
- must not share a complete sub-expression of 4 or more
  nodes with any published Alpha101 formula, or with any factor already in the
  archive. Restating a published alpha is the one thing that is always rejected.
- must cover at least 90% of the panel
- absolute rank correlation below 0.80 against every archive member

Output
- Return valid JSON only, matching the supplied JSON schema. No prose outside it.


TASK: MUTATE. For each parent below, identify its single weakest component and
change ONLY that component.

A mutation is localized: the returned expression must be within
3 tree edits of its parent. Rewriting the idea is not a mutation
and will be rejected. Say which node you changed in `changed_node`, and put the
parent's id in `parent_ids`.

Read the diagnostics: a factor whose IC is positive in most years and negative in two has a regime problem, one with high turnover is paying costs it does not earn back, and one whose IC half-life is short is being asked to predict too far ahead. Change the component responsible for the specific weakness you name.

  1.   2. Small edits to an already-archived formula, one operand or one window changed, still overlap heavily in structure and get caught as a near-duplicate; when reusing a family that's already in the archive, change the functional form (e.g. normalize by dispersion instead of range) rather than tweaking a single parameter.
  3. In ratio-style factors (return sum scaled by volatility), keep numerator and denominator on the same lookback window; a short-over-long mismatch (3-day sum over 21-day std) failed the cheap screen far worse than a matched long-over-long version (126-day over 126-day) that got accepted.
  4. Multiplying two independently-ranked short-horizon sub-factors (a short return-sum rank times a volatility-ratio rank) nearly cancelled out to zero signal this round; treat that combination pattern as low-probability unless each sub-factor already shows signal on its own.
  5. Lookback windows approaching 200 days are cutting it close on coverage for this universe and period; the longest window accepted this round was 126 days, so anything beyond that needs an explicit coverage check before proposing.
  6. Piecewise return transforms (clipping to positive-only, or taking absolute value) combined into a ratio at a 21-day window landed just under the cheap-window bar; this shape needs a different window or a simpler transform before resubmitting.
  7. Standalone timing-of-extremum features (where in a long window the min or max occurred) showed almost no signal alone this round; don't resubmit these without pairing them with a stronger co-factor.
  8. The strongest results this round normalized a price or range value by dispersion measured over that same single window rather than mixing two separate windows; favor this self-normalization pattern for price_volume niches over multi-window combinations.
